accroche: The sentence means absolutely nothing. Yet it is perfectly grammatical, and that is exactly why Noam Chomsky chose it, in 1957.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” (in French, “d'incolores idées vertes dorment furieusement”). Nothing in the world corresponds to a green idea, let alone a colorless one, and an idea does not sleep, furiously or otherwise. The sentence makes no sense. Yet any speaker of English immediately recognizes it as well formed. We know it is grammatical without knowing what it is about. This is the sentence that linguist Noam Chomsky chose, in 1957, to open a chapter of his book *Syntactic Structures*.

## A Sentence Built to Mean Nothing

Chomsky sets against it a second sequence, made of the same five words in scrambled order: “furiously sleep ideas green colorless.” This one, every speaker of English immediately rejects as ill formed. Yet the two sentences share one essential trait: neither has ever been uttered before in an English text or conversation. A model that judged a sentence's grammaticality by the statistical frequency of word sequences observed in vast corpora (the dominant approach at the time, inherited from information theory) would assign both sentences an equally near-zero probability, since neither has ever appeared. Such a model therefore cannot explain why one is accepted and the other rejected: both look equally foreign to English.

## What This Shifts

The example isolates, with rare sharpness, three notions that we spontaneously confuse: being grammatically correct, having a meaning, and being a sequence of words already encountered. A sentence can be well formed without meaning anything, like the green ideas; a sequence of words can have never been uttered without that stopping it from being recognized as perfectly English; and meaning, or the lack of it, does not depend at all on the order in which the words appear. Only grammaticality depends on it. This dissociation becomes one of the founding arguments of generative grammar: syntax, for Chomsky, obeys rules of its own, independent of the meaning of the words it organizes, and which no frequency count is enough to describe. A sentence can therefore be at once pure nonsense and a model of grammar: the two judgments are made on planes that do not overlap.

carte.punch: A sentence with no meaning at all, yet perfectly grammatical: Chomsky made it up on purpose, in 1957.
carte.idee: “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” means nothing, but every English speaker recognizes it as grammatical, unlike those same words in scrambled order. Chomsky draws a theoretical argument from it: grammaticality, meaning, and frequency of use are three distinct things.

quiz.question: Why does Chomsky choose a nonsensical sentence (“colorless green ideas sleep furiously”) rather than a sensible one to illustrate his argument?
choix: Because all the sensible sentences of English had already been used as examples by other linguists, and Chomsky wanted a novel example
Because it lets him show that a sentence can be grammatically correct without having any meaning, which a sensible sentence could not have demonstrated as clearly
Because Chomsky was trying to demonstrate that standard English actually allows word combinations wrongly believed to be absurd
Because the meaning of a sentence, according to Chomsky, depends solely on word order, not on the individual meaning of the words
quiz.explication: By choosing a nonsensical sentence, Chomsky isolates grammaticality from meaning: a sensible sentence would not have made it possible to tell which of the two criteria is really at play. It is not a matter of the example's originality: Chomsky looks instead for a nonsense recognized as such, not a combination wrongly judged absurd. And he never claims that meaning depends on word order: it is grammaticality, distinct from meaning, that varies with that order in his example.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the two word sequences that Chomsky contrasts have in common?
choix: Both are judged grammatical by English speakers
Neither had ever been uttered before in English
Both have a meaning, but one that is hard to grasp at first
Both already appeared in information-theory corpora
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Neither “colorless green ideas sleep furiously” nor its scrambled version had ever been said or written in English. That is exactly what makes the example decisive: the two sequences are equally unprecedented, and yet only one is accepted.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does a model that judges grammaticality by the frequency of word sequences fail here?
choix: Because it assigns both sequences an equally near-zero probability
Because no corpus of written English was large enough in 1957
Because it confuses nouns and verbs in short sentences
Because it rejects on principle any sentence without meaning
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Since both sequences are equally absent from corpora, a frequency-based model treats them alike: it therefore cannot explain why an English speaker accepts the first and rejects the second.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What changes when the same five words are put in scrambled order?
choix: The meaning of the sequence, which becomes interpretable in another way
Its frequency in corpora, which rises markedly
Its grammaticality, but not its lack of meaning
Nothing: the two sequences are judged equivalent
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The example dissociates three things we spontaneously confuse: being grammatical, having a meaning, and having already been heard. The nonsense remains intact in both sequences; only grammaticality depends on word order.
